1.pericope_label: Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say... The Lord is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked

schools.summary: Delitzsch places the psalm by its neighbours — the earlier pair ran let Israel say then peace be upon Israel, and here the order reverses — hears a deliverance already experienced looked back on gratefully, and corrects the word rendered furrow: it is not the furrow but the strip of land a ploughman takes at one time, at each end of which the team halts and turns. Ellicott reaches the same result from Wettstein, flattens two phrases (the youth is the nation's, the original has no adverb of time), calls the double image of verse 3 as striking as poetry ever produced, and finds in the unconjoined statement that the Lord is righteous a revelation of how deep Israel's religion ran.

Calvin states the psalm's purpose as doctrine — God subjects his church to troubles so that he may better prove himself her deliverer, and we despair only because present evils engross us and we forget that the fathers' patience was tried the same way — dates it to the years after the return when the Jews had almost fainted under Antiochus, and notices that the enemies are named by a bare pronoun, which aggravates the evil. Gill hears the Messiah in the ploughed back and finds mercy in the Hebrew word for righteousness.

Clarke dates the writing after the captivity, reads the ploughing as a yoke to which the people were themselves harnessed, as Jerome took it, and refuses the application of verse 3 to Christ's scourging for want of any authority. Wesley glosses the cords as the enemies' plots and righteous as merciful.

Henry has the church speak as one aged person recalling former days, and notices that the metaphors of Psalm 125 and this psalm are crossed — the rod where one expects the plough, the plough where one expects the rod — reading the tearing as a wearing out of the saints which God permitted so that the broken fallow might take the seeds of his grace. Spurgeon explains the psalm's vagueness: Israel says they because it would be impossible to know all their names, and persecution is the heirloom of the church and the ensign of the elect.

Augustine traces the speaking church back past Israel: it is of ancient birth, and was once in Abel only, fought against by his lost brother, and once in Enoch alone. Like Zacchaeus, little of stature but mighty in works, the psalm is short in words and large in sentiment.

positions.summary: Israel's, and beyond that the Messiah's, who gave his back to the smiters — alongside the Israelites scourged under the Maccabees, and the tradition that a Roman general ploughed up Jerusalem.
Not Christ's: the words have been applied to his sufferings, but on no known authority, since no such scourging could have taken place when it is not likely he received more than thirty-nine stripes.
The nation's, as a double image at once of the lash across a slave's back and of the imprints of oppression left on the country as on the race.
The church's in every age, torn as a husbandman tears ground with the share, to wear the saints out as long-tilled ground is worn out of heart.

debates.question: When was the psalm written, and what does 'from my youth' reach back to?

positions.summary: After the captivity; the youth is the earliest part of the nation's history, the bondage in Egypt.
In the years after the return, when the Jews had almost fainted under the tyranny of Antiochus Epiphanes and the church stood on the verge of total destruction.
The youth is Israel's in Egypt or in the times of the Judges, but the gospel-church bore the same yoke most of all in its own youth, witness the ten persecutions.
Further back than Israel: the church was already being fought against when it consisted of Abel alone.

outliers.summary: Distinguishes the cause of the church's sufferings from their occasion: they brought their troubles on themselves by their sins, but what their neighbours hated them for was the peculiarity of their covenant.

Corrects the agricultural term: the word is not the furrow but the strip of arable land the ploughman takes in hand at one time, at either end of which the team comes to a stand, turns round, and begins a new furrow.

themes: Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say:
Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth: yet they have not prevailed against me.
The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows.
The Lord is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked.

5.pericope_label: Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion... neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the Lord be upon you

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out both sides of the disputed clause in verse 6. Its Aramaic colouring probably conceals a textual error, and the context seems to want 'before it is plucked up', a sense extracted from a verb used elsewhere of drawing a sword or plucking off a shoe and read impersonally, with the Greek, Vulgate and Theodotion behind it; but grass withering before maturity, growing without soil like the seed on the rock, is exactly what the passage expects and implies a more sudden destruction, so he keeps the received rendering, which Aquila, Symmachus and some Greek readings support.

Gill supplies the natural history of a flat plastered roof and then two travellers' reports — Menochius on the earthen roofs of Corsica, and Olaus Magnus on the northern Gothic houses turfed and sown with barley so that they look like green meadows and are watered against withering — and measures the failure by the harvest: such grass never rises high enough to be mowed, nor is there enough to fill a mower's hand.

Clarke explains that seeds arriving by accident on a roof vegetate imperfectly, so that the mower can make no hay and the reaper no sheaf, and applies it: let the Babylonians be like such herbage. He glosses the disputed verb as before it is unsheathed, that is, before it ears, and reads the missing harvest-greeting as a curse of desolation which he says has literally befallen Babylon. Wesley states the conclusion flatly: having no deep root the grass never comes to maturity, and so all their designs shall be abortive.

Henry hears the psalm end as Deborah's song ended, takes the imprecation as prediction, and sets the loaded palm and fruitful olive against grass that is little, short, sour and good for nothing — the higher its position, which is perhaps its pride, the more exposed to the sun. On the last verse he turns the custom into two warnings: sacred expressions must not be used in light and ludicrous actions, and it is dangerous to wish the church's enemies well in what they attempt.

debates.question: Does the grass wither before it is plucked, or before it comes to maturity?

positions.summary: Before it comes to maturity — the received rendering, which suits grass growing without soil and implies a more sudden destruction, and is supported by Aquila, Symmachus and some Greek readings.

Before it is plucked up — the sense the context seems to require, got by reading impersonally a verb used elsewhere of drawing a sword or plucking off a shoe, and favoured by the Greek received text, the Vulgate and Theodotion.
Before it is unsheathed, that is, before it ears.

debates.question: What is the force of the withheld harvest blessing?

positions.summary: A curse of desolation on the land, so that no harvest ever appears in it again — which has literally befallen Babylon, where no harvests grow near the place it stood.

Two moral warnings: sacred expressions must never be used in light and ludicrous actions, since mowing a house-top would be a jest; and whoever bids the church's enemies God speed is partaker of their evil deeds.
The absence of an ordinary courtesy: the scene is exactly that of Boaz and his reapers, and the closing line should be printed as the reapers' return greeting.

outliers.summary: Observes that the church's enemies wither of themselves and do not wait to be rooted out by the judgments of God.

Reports from Olaus Magnus that in the northern Gothic countries cattle are fed on the tops of the houses, especially during a siege, the roofs being turfed and sown with barley or oats so that they look like green meadows and are watered daily to keep them from withering — the exact reverse of the psalm's image.

themes: Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion.
Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up:
Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom.
Neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the Lord be upon you: we bless you in the name of the Lord.
